Live, multi-camera tracking with SAM 2, on one GPU or many. SAM 2 and its smaller sibling EdgeTAM can track anything you point at, but their code was written for one recorded video at a time. tamserve is the serving engine they are missing: one copy of the model tracks every object on every camera, for as long as the cameras run. Point at what to track, or name it ("dog", "the red mug") and tamserve finds it. Why tamserve · New to video tracking? · Using it · Tracking by name · How it works · Results · Limits Six live cameras on one GPU, every one at 30 frames/s. Watch the 32-second demo , or read how it was recorded . The models are excellent. The code that comes with them was made for editing one recorded video, and the usual way to put it on several cameras is to run a separate copy of the model for each one. Memory piles up with every copy and with every minute of video. tamserve does what LLM servers such as vLLM do for chat: every camera shares one copy of the model, and whatever needs the GPU at a given moment goes through it together. That turns out to be faster as well as lighter, and because the model itself is not touched, the results are the same. These are for EdgeTAM on one RTX 4090, against EdgeTAM's own code at its fastest: compiled, one copy per camera, all sharing the GPU. Speeds are totals across the cameras, with one object each. With the larger SAM 2.1 models, tamserve runs at the same speed as Meta's current SAM 2 code and uses about a third of the GPU memory. Results has the full tables. Say you have video, and you need to know where one particular thing is in every frame: this person, that forklift, the dog. That is tracking. SAM 2 and its smaller relatives, EdgeTAM and SAM 2.1, are models from Meta that do it very well. You point at the thing once, on a single frame, and the model draws its exact outline on every frame after that. tamserve sits between one of those models and your program. Your program hands it the latest frame from each camera and gets back the outline of every tracked object in each one. You can start tracking something new, or stop, at any moment, and cameras can come and go. It is meant for anyone who has to answer "where exactly is this thing, right now, in each of my video feeds": sports and broadcast graphics, warehouse and retail analytics, robotics, wildlife and lab monitoring, annotation tools. There are two ways to say what to track. You can point: a person clicking on the picture, or a detector, says where the thing is, and tamserve takes over from there. Or you can name it: a Tracker takes a word or a phrase, finds everything that matches on every camera, and follows it. Four words come up a lot below: pip install tamserve You need Python 3.10 or newer and an NVIDIA GPU. It does run on a CPU, which is handy for trying it out but much too slow for live video. The first time you load a model, tamserve downloads it into ~/.cache/tamserve , so that run needs an internet connection. EdgeTAM is 54 MB. The download is pinned to one version and verified before any of it is loaded. tamserve does not open cameras, and it does not run a loop of its own. Your program reads frames however it likes and calls engine.step() once per round, with the newest frame from each camera exactly as the decoder gives it. This example uses OpenCV to read two network cameras: import threading import cv2 # pip install opencv-python; any source of frames will do from tamserve import Box , Engine , build_video_predictor class Camera : """Reads one stream on a thread of its own and keeps its newest frame.""" def __init__ ( self , url ): self . stream , self . newest , self . arrived = cv2 . VideoCapture ( url ), None , threading . Event () threading . Thread ( target = self . read , daemon = True ). start () def read ( self ): while True : ok , picture = self . stream . read () if not ok : break # the stream has ended self . newest = cv2 . cvtColor ( picture , cv2 . COLOR_BGR2RGB ) # OpenCV gives BGR, the engine takes RGB self . arrived . set () def take ( self ): """Waits for a frame the loop has not seen yet, and returns it.""" self . arrived . wait () self . arrived . clear () return self . newest engine = Engine ( build_video_predictor ( "cuda" )) # loads EdgeTAM onto the GPU cameras = { "door" : Camera ( "rtsp://door-camera/stream" ), "yard" : Camera ( "rtsp://yard-camera/stream" )} # What to track and where it is in the first frame: a box as (left, top, right, bottom), in pixels. # In a real system this comes from a detector, or from someone drawing on the picture. start = { "door" : { "courier" : Box ( 410 , 120 , 560 , 480 )}} while True : # 1. Take the newest frame from each camera. frames = { name : camera . take () for name , camera in cameras . items ()} # 2. One call tracks every object in every one of those frames. masks = engine . step ( frames , start ) start = None # the box was only needed once; from here on the engine tracks the courier by itself # 3. Use the answer. masks["door"]["courier"] is True on the courier's pixels and False everywhere else. for camera_name , objects in masks . items (): for object_name , mask in objects . items (): print ( camera_name , object_name , "covers" , int ( mask . sum ()), "pixels" ) Each call to step() takes one frame per camera and returns when the masks for those frames are ready. The engine remembers what it is tracking between calls, which is why the box is passed only once. Camera names and object names are yours to choose. The frames go in exactly as the decoder gives them. The engine uploads them and resizes them on the GPU, which takes about half a millisecond a frame where resizing on the CPU takes 16. The Camera class is there for speed too: with a thread per camera, the next round's frames are decoded while the GPU tracks this one. And because a camera keeps only its newest frame, a loop that falls behind skips frames and does not lag. The engine tracks from whatever frame it is given and does not need to see every one. How fast can the loop go? On an RTX 4090 with the compiled engine, eight 720p cameras and one object each, a loop like this one tracks 273 frames a second from video to masks, which is 34 for every camera. With 1080p cameras it is 238. To start tracking something, you give it a name and point at it in the current frame. There are three ways to point. All of them use the frame's own pixel coordinates, with x counted from the left edge and y from the top. Start tracking something. Pass its name and where it is, together with the frame it is in. You do this once. Everything already being tracked carries on undisturbed. engine . step ( frames , { "yard" : { "dog" : Box ( 300 , 380 , 420 , 470 )}}) Stop tracking something. engine . drop ( "door" , "courier" ) # just the courier engine . drop ( "door" ) # everything on the door camera Fix a track that has gone wrong. Now and then an outline drifts. It slides onto the wrong person, or keeps only half of the object. Point at the object again under the same name, exactly as you did to start it. Tracking begins afresh from the new box, and the old, mistaken history is thrown away. engine . step ( frames , { "door" : { "courier" : Box ( 455 , 130 , 600 , 500 )}}) # same name, new box Start something you noticed in the frame you just processed. step() moves every tracked object forward by one frame. Suppose a detector looked at the frame you just passed in and found a dog. Calling step() again with that same frame would move everything else forward twice. add() starts the dog on that frame and leaves the rest alone. engine . add ( frames , { "yard" : { "dog" : Box ( 300 , 380 , 420 , 470 )}}) # frames: the ones you just gave step() Following what you name Everything above starts from someone pointing at the thing. A Tracker takes words instead. Give it a phrase, or several, and it finds every match on every camera, follows each one, picks up new ones as they appear and lets go of those that leave. One live camera on one RTX 4090. The words are set while it runs, and nobody points at anything. Watch the 17-second clip , read how it was recorded , or try it in Colab . from tamserve import Engine , Tracker , build_video_predictor engine = Engine ( build_video_predictor ( "cuda" , "sam2.1-large" ), compile = True ) tracker = Tracker ( engine , { "door" : [ "person" , "package" ], "yard" : "dog" }) # loads SAM 3, the model that finds things while True : frames = { name : camera . take () for name , camera in cameras . items ()} # as in the live loop above masks = tracker . step ( frames ) # masks["door"] is {1: mask, 2: mask, 3: mask}: one mask for everything found on the door camera # tracker.names("door") is {1: "person", 2: "person", 3: "package"}: what each of them is For the same phrase on every camera, Tracker(engine, "dog") is enough. Each thing gets a number, counted from 1 on each camera, and keeps it for as long as it is followed. It works by pairing two models. SAM 3 is Meta's model that outlines whatever you name. It is accurate and slow: one look at one frame takes about 65 ms on an RTX 4090. The model inside the engine cannot find anything by itself, but it follows what it is given far more cheaply, a few ms a frame with EdgeTAM and a few tens with SAM 2.1 large. So SAM 3 looks at each camera once every three frames, the engine follows what it found in between, and the looks are spread out so that they never all land in the same round. SAM 3 can also follow things through a video by itself. Here are the two side by side on one RTX 4090, on 117 videos from Meta's own benchmark for SAM 3, each paired with phrases such as "the white scarf" (224 pairs, none of them used to choose any setting). The security cameras are a second set of videos: HOTA is the usual score for tracking, from 0 to 100. It combines how well things are found with how well each one keeps the same number. So Tracker gives up a few points of accuracy and costs two fifths as much, or a quarter with EdgeTAM. It also does three things SAM 3's tracker cannot: it runs many cameras at once, it asks one camera for several things at little extra cost, and its memory does not grow with the video. Results has the full tables. Tracker and PeopleTracker are add-ons. They need Meta's SAM 3, which does not come with tamserve unless you ask for it: pip install " tamserve[sam3] " hf auth login # once: SAM 3's weights are gated Before the weights will download, accept Meta's licence on the facebook/sam3 page on Hugging Face. They are 3.5 GB and are fetched the first time a tracker starts. SAM 3 has its own licence, which is not Apache-2.0, so read it before you build on it. People are what cameras are most often asked about, so they have a tracker of their own. A PeopleTracker works as a Tracker does, with rules tuned on people: it looks five times less often, and it is both more accurate and far cheaper than SAM 3's own tracker. from tamserve import Engine , PeopleTracker , build_video_predictor engine = Engine ( build_video_predictor ( "cuda" ), compile = True ) people = PeopleTracker ( engine ) # loads SAM 3, the model that finds the people while True : frames = { name : camera . take () for name , camera in cameras . items ()} # as in the live loop above masks = people . step ( frames ) # masks["door"] is {1: mask, 2: mask}: one mask for each person in view on the door camera Each person gets a number, counted from 1 on each camera, and keeps it for as long as they are followed. Someone hidden for a moment, behind a door or another person, has the same number when they reappear. It pairs the same two models. People move slowly against the size of a picture and SAM 3 is sure of them, so one look every 15 frames is enough, and EdgeTAM, the smallest model, follows them for about 4 ms a frame. SAM 3 can also track people through a video by itself. Here are the two side by side, on one RTX 4090 and the same videos: Results has the full tables. Engine(predictor, compile=True) compiles the model for your GPU. Every speed figure on this page uses it, and the price is a slow first start. Later starts are quick because PyTorch keeps the compiled code on disk. By default it keeps it in /tmp , so point TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR at a folder that survives a reboot. Compiling has only been tested on Linux. One engine drives one GPU. For several, on one machine or many, use a Router . It runs a worker on each GPU, puts each camera on the one with the most room, and gives you every camera's results in one place. Each worker opens and decodes its own cameras, so video never travels between them. from tamserve import Box , Router def main (): router = Router ( compile = True ) # a worker on every GPU this machine has router . add_camera ( "dock-1" , "rtsp://10.1.0.21/stream" ) router . add_camera ( "dock-2" , "rtsp://10.1.0.22/stream" ) router . start ( "dock-1" , "forklift" , Box ( 410 , 120 , 560 , 480 )) for update in router . results (): # every camera, whichever GPU tracked it for name , mask in update . masks . items (): print ( update . camera , update . frame , name , mask . box , mask . area ) if __name__ == "__main__" : # each worker is a new Python process, and it imports this file as it starts main () The router reads the cameras itself, so you give it each camera's address instead of handing it frames. Opening streams by address needs OpenCV ( pip install opencv-python-headless ). start() , stop() and remove_camera() work as on an engine. On two RTX 4090s, with one object per camera, a router tracked 476 frames a second from 32 cameras of 720p video, against 241 on one GPU. A router keeps going when a camera drops or a worker stops, and its workers can be on other machines: Several GPUs covers both. For every frame, a SAM 2-style tracker encodes the image, looks the object up in its memory of recent frames, draws the mask, and writes the frame into that memory. tamserve runs those same four modules, once per step, over every object on every camera. flowchart LR A[Newest frame from

one row per object] M[(Per-object memory
prompt frame, 6 frames,
15 summaries)] --> C C --> D[Mask decoder] D --> E[Masks out] D --> F[Memory encoder] F --> M Loading Five things make that fast. None of them changes what the model computes; at most they change floating-point rounding. The full account is in docs/how-it-works.md . What each change bought, and what was tried and dropped, is in docs/results.md . The table under Why tamserve is the short version, and the sections on naming things and people have their own. Every measurement, with the machine it ran on and the command that reproduces it, is in docs/results.md : speed from 1 to 64 cameras, accuracy for all five models, memory, SAM 2.1 against Meta's current code, live video, two GPUs, and both trackers against SAM 3's own. What tamserve does not do: What to expect in practice: Created by Aryaman Darda . tamserve is Apache-2.0. It runs EdgeTAM and SAM 2.1 by Meta, both Apache-2.0, which it downloads and does not redistribute. Accuracy is measured on DAVIS 2017 , which is for research use; check its licence before using it for anything else. Tracker and PeopleTracker call Meta's SAM 3 , which has its own licence, is not part of tamserve, and is only installed and downloaded when you ask for it. They are scored on SA-Co/VEval , BURST , MOTS20 and MOT20 and MEVA (CC BY 4.0), each under its own terms.
